answer_text:
- Demonstrate that the data subject has consented to the processing (Art. 7.1; Rec. 42).

- If consent is given in a written declaration that also concerns other matters:
  - present the request for consent in a manner clearly distinguishable from the other matters, in an intelligible and easily accessible form, using clear and plain language (Art. 7.2; Rec. 42);
  - any part of such a declaration that infringes the Regulation is not binding (Art. 7.2).

- Ensure consent is informed by making the data subject aware at least of the identity of the controller and the purposes of the processing (Rec. 42).

- Ensure consent is freely given:
  - take utmost account of whether performance of a contract or provision of a service is conditional on consent to processing that is not necessary for that contract or service (Art. 7.4);
  - do not rely on consent where the data subject has no genuine or free choice or is unable to refuse or withdraw consent without detriment (Rec. 42).

- Inform the data subject, prior to giving consent, that they have the right to withdraw consent at any time; make withdrawal as easy as giving consent; withdrawal does not affect the lawfulness of processing based on consent before its withdrawal (Art. 7.3; Rec. 42).

- When using pre-formulated (controller‑provided) declarations, ensure they are intelligible, easily accessible, use clear and plain language and do not contain unfair terms (Rec. 42).

question: What are the obligations of the data controller when the legal basis for the data processing is the consent of the data subject?
answer_text:
- Processing may be based on the data subject's consent only where the data subject has given consent for one or more specific purposes (G Art. 6.1(a)).

- The controller must be able to demonstrate that the data subject has consented to the processing (G Art. 7.1; G Rec. 42).

- Consent must be informed: the data subject should be aware at least of the identity of the controller and the purposes of the processing (G Rec. 42).

- Where consent is given by a pre‑formulated declaration, the controller must provide it in an intelligible and easily accessible form, using clear and plain language and not containing unfair terms (G Rec. 42).

- The controller must ensure safeguards so that, especially when consent is bundled with another matter, the data subject is aware of the fact and extent of the consent (G Rec. 42).

- Consent must be freely given: it is not to be regarded as freely given if the data subject lacks a genuine or free choice or is unable to refuse or withdraw consent without detriment (G Rec. 42).

question: What are the obligations of the data controller when the legal basis for the data processing is the consent of the data subject?
answer_text:
When processing is based on the data subject's consent, the controller must:

- Be able to demonstrate that the data subject has consented to the processing. (G Art.7.1; G Rec.42)

- If consent is given in a written declaration that also concerns other matters, present the request for consent in a way that is clearly distinguishable from the other matters, intelligible and easily accessible, using clear and plain language; any part of such a declaration that infringes the Regulation is not binding. (G Art.7.2; G Rec.42)

- Inform the data subject prior to giving consent (including, at least, the identity of the controller and the purposes of the processing). (G Art.7.3; G Rec.42)

- Give the data subject the right to withdraw consent at any time; withdrawal must be as easy as giving consent and does not affect the lawfulness of processing carried out on the basis of consent before its withdrawal. (G Art.7.3)

- When assessing whether consent is freely given, take utmost account of, inter alia, whether performance of a contract (including provision of a service) is made conditional on consent to processing that is not necessary for performance of that contract; ensure consent is a genuine, free choice and that the data subject can refuse or withdraw without detriment. (G Art.7.4; G Rec.42)

- Ensure any controller‑preformulated declaration of consent is intelligible, easily accessible, uses clear and plain language, and does not contain unfair terms; provide safeguards so the data subject is aware of the fact and extent of the consent. (G Rec.42)

(Consent is one lawful basis for processing under the Regulation. G Art.6.1(a))

question: What are the obligations of the data controller when the legal basis for the data processing is the consent of the data subject?
answer_text:
- Legal basis: consent is one of the lawful bases for processing (G Art. 6.1(a)).  
- Burden of proof: the controller must be able to demonstrate that the data subject has consented (G Art. 7.1; G Rec. 42).  
- Form and evidencing of consent:
  - Consent must be given by a clear affirmative act establishing a freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous indication of agreement (G Rec. 32).  
  - Silence, pre‑ticked boxes or inactivity do not constitute consent (G Rec. 32).  
  - Where consent is given in the context of a written declaration on another matter, safeguards must ensure the data subject is aware that and to what extent consent is given (G Rec. 42).  
  - A pre‑formulated declaration of consent must be intelligible and easily accessible, using clear and plain language and must not contain unfair terms (G Rec. 42).  
- Content of the information supporting consent: the data subject should be aware at least of the identity of the controller and the purposes of the processing (G Rec. 42).  
- Scope and granularity:
  - Consent should cover all processing activities carried out for the same purpose(s); if processing has multiple purposes, consent must be given for all of them (G Rec. 32).  
  - Separate consent should be possible for different processing operations where appropriate; consent is presumed not freely given if it does not allow such separate consent when appropriate (G Rec. 43).  
- Freely given requirement:
  - Consent must be freely given; it is not freely given where there is a clear imbalance between data subject and controller (in particular where the controller is a public authority) or where the data subject has no genuine or free choice (G Rec. 43; G Rec. 42).  
  - Consent is not freely given if the performance of a contract or provision of a service is made conditional on consent that is not necessary for that performance (G Rec. 43).  
- Electronic requests: if consent is requested by electronic means, the request must be clear, concise and not unnecessarily disruptive to the use of the service (G Rec. 32).  
- Withdrawal: consent should not be regarded as freely given if the data subject is unable to refuse or withdraw consent without detriment — the controller must not place the data subject in that position (G Rec. 42).

question: What are the obligations of the data controller when the legal basis for the data processing is the consent of the data subject?
answer_text:
- Use consent as the legal basis only where the data subject has given consent for one or more specific purposes (G Art.6.1(a)).

- Be able to demonstrate that the data subject has consented to the processing (G Art.7.1; G Rec.42).

- Where consent is given in a written declaration on another matter, ensure safeguards so the data subject is aware of the fact that and the extent to which consent is given (G Rec.42).

- Provide pre‑formulated declarations in an intelligible and easily accessible form, using clear and plain language and without unfair terms (G Rec.42).

- Ensure consent is informed by making the data subject aware at least of the identity of the controller and the purposes of the processing (G Rec.42).

- Ensure consent is freely given; it is not freely given where the data subject has no genuine or free choice or is unable to refuse or withdraw consent without detriment (G Rec.42).

question: Which legal entity can impose fines on data controllers?
answer_text: - The supervisory authority (each supervisory authority) — it has the power to impose administrative fines pursuant to Article 83 (G Art. 58; G Art. 83).

question: Which legal entity can impose fines on data controllers?
answer_text: The supervisory authority (each supervisory authority) can impose administrative fines on controllers (and processors). (G Art. 58.2 point (i); G Rec. 148; G Art. 83.2)

question: Which legal entity can impose fines on data controllers?
answer_text:
- The supervisory authority (i.e. each supervisory authority) can impose administrative fines on controllers or processors (G Art. 58.2(i); G Art. 83).  
- This is reflected in the recital that penalties, including administrative fines, should be imposed by the supervisory authority (G Rec. 148).

question: Which legal entity can impose fines on data controllers?
answer_text:
- Supervisory authority: each supervisory authority has the power to impose administrative fines (G Art. 58.2 (i); G Rec. 150).  
- Exception where national law bars administrative fines: in Member States whose legal system does not provide for administrative fines, the fine may be imposed by competent national courts (with initiation by the supervisory authority) (G Art. 83.9; G Rec. 151).

question: Which legal entity can impose fines on data controllers?
answer_text:
- The supervisory authority (each supervisory authority) may impose administrative fines on controllers pursuant to G Art. 58 (2)(i).  
- The rules on such administrative fines are set out in G Art. 83.2.

question: Who can exercise the right to lodge a complaint before the supervisory authority?
answer_text:
- Every data subject has the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority (in particular in the Member State of his or her habitual residence, place of work, or place of the alleged infringement) if they consider that processing of their personal data infringes the Regulation (Art. 77.1).

- Complaints may also be lodged by a body, organisation or association, as provided for in Article 80 (Art. 57.1(f); Art. 57.2).

question: Who can exercise the right to lodge a complaint before the supervisory authority?
answer_text:
- Who: every data subject (G Art. 77.1; G Rec. 141).  
- When: if the data subject considers that the processing of personal data relating to him or her infringes this Regulation (G Art. 77.1).  
- Where: the complaint may be lodged in particular in the Member State of the data subject’s habitual residence, place of work or place of the alleged infringement (G Art. 77.1; G Rec. 141).

question: Who can exercise the right to lodge a complaint before the supervisory authority?
answer_text: - Every data subject may exercise the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority (in particular in the Member State of his or her habitual residence, place of work or place of the alleged infringement) — G Art. 77.1; see also G Rec. 141.

question: Who can exercise the right to lodge a complaint before the supervisory authority?
answer_text:
- Every data subject has the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority (in particular in the Member State of his or her habitual residence, place of work or place of the alleged infringement) (G Art. 77.1; G Rec. 141).  
- A data subject may mandate a properly constituted not‑for‑profit body, organisation or association (with public‑interest statutory objectives and active in data‑protection) to lodge a complaint and to exercise the rights in Articles 77–79 on their behalf (G Art. 80.1; G Rec. 142).  
- In addition, a Member State may provide that such a not‑for‑profit body may have the right to lodge a complaint in that Member State independently of a data subject’s mandate (G Rec. 142).

question: Who can exercise the right to lodge a complaint before the supervisory authority?
answer_text: - Every data subject who considers that the processing of personal data relating to him or her infringes this Regulation may lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority (in particular in the Member State of his or her habitual residence, place of work or place of the alleged infringement) (G Art. 77.1; see also G Rec. 141).

question: What is the procedure to follow in the event of a data breach?
answer_text:
- Detect and escalate internally: the processor must notify the controller without undue delay after becoming aware of a personal data breach (G Art. 33.2).

- Notify the competent supervisory authority: the controller shall notify the personal data breach to the supervisory authority competent in accordance with Article 55 without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it (G Art. 33.1; G Art. 55.1).

- Include required information in the notification: the notification to the supervisory authority shall, where possible, (a) describe the nature of the breach including categories and approximate numbers of data subjects and records concerned, (b) give the name and contact details of the data protection officer or other contact point, (c) describe the likely consequences of the breach, and (d) describe measures taken or proposed to address the breach and mitigate adverse effects (G Art. 33.3).

- Provide information in phases if necessary: if it is not possible to provide all information at once, the information may be provided in phases without undue further delay (G Art. 33.4).

- Keep records: the controller shall document any personal data breaches, comprising the facts, its effects and the remedial action taken, so the supervisory authority can verify compliance (G Art. 33.5).

- Communicate to data subjects when required: the controller should communicate the breach to the data subject without undue delay where the breach is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of the natural person; that communication should describe the nature of the breach and give recommendations to mitigate potential adverse effects, and be made as soon as reasonably feasible in close cooperation with the supervisory authority and other relevant authorities (G Rec. 86).

- Take and check protective measures and consider other interests: appropriate technical and organisational measures should be in place to detect breaches and enable prompt notification; the assessment of whether notification was made without undue delay should take account of the nature and gravity of the breach; and rules on timing/format should consider whether technical protections limit risk and whether early disclosure would hamper law‑enforcement investigations (G Rec. 87; G Rec. 88; G Rec. 85).

question: What is the procedure to follow in the event of a data breach?
answer_text:
- Detect and assess the breach and the measures in place to detect it (technological and organisational measures) (G Rec. 87).
- Notify the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after becoming aware of the breach (G Art. 33.1; G Rec. 85).
  - If the controller can demonstrate that the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, notification is not required (G Rec. 85).
  - If notification cannot be made within 72 hours, the reasons for the delay must accompany the notification and information may be provided in phases (G Rec. 85).
  - The fact that notification was made without undue delay is assessed having regard to the nature and gravity of the breach and its consequences (G Rec. 87).
  - Notification may lead to intervention by the supervisory authority (G Rec. 87).
- Communicate to the data subject without undue delay where the breach is likely to result in a high risk to their rights and freedoms; the communication should describe the nature of the breach and give recommendations to mitigate adverse effects (G Rec. 86).
  - Such communications should be made as soon as reasonably feasible and in close cooperation with the supervisory authority and, where relevant, law‑enforcement authorities, taking account of any guidance they provide (G Rec. 86).
- When setting the format and timing of notifications and communications, take into account the circumstances of the breach (including whether data were protected by effective technical measures) and the legitimate interests of law‑enforcement where early disclosure could hamper investigations (G Rec. 88).

question: What is the procedure to follow in the event of a data breach?
answer_text:
- Detect and have measures in place to enable rapid detection and notification of a breach (technological and organisational measures) (G Rec. 87).

- If you are a processor: notify the controller without undue delay after becoming aware of a personal data breach (G Art. 33.2).

- If you are the controller: notify the competent supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after becoming aware of the breach (G Art. 33.1; G Rec. 85). If you can demonstrate the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to rights and freedoms, notification is not required (G Rec. 85).

- If notification cannot be given within 72 hours, include the reasons for the delay with the notification; information may be provided in phases without undue further delay (G Rec. 85; G Art. 33.4).

- Ensure the notification to the supervisory authority describes:
  - the nature of the personal data breach, including, where possible, categories and approximate number of data subjects and of personal data records concerned;
  - the name and contact details of the data protection officer or other contact point;
  - the likely consequences of the personal data breach;
  - the measures taken or proposed to address the breach, including measures to mitigate possible adverse effects (G Art. 33.3).

- Document every personal data breach, recording the facts, its effects and the remedial action taken; documentation must enable the supervisory authority to verify compliance (G Art. 33.5).

- If the breach is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of data subjects, communicate the breach to the data subjects without undue delay, describing the nature of the breach and recommendations to mitigate adverse effects; such communications should be made as soon as reasonably feasible and in close cooperation with the supervisory authority, respecting its guidance and that of relevant authorities (e.g. law enforcement) (G Rec. 86; G Rec. 88).

question: What is the procedure to follow in the event of a data breach?
answer_text:
- Immediate internal step: the processor must notify the controller without undue delay after becoming aware of a personal data breach. (G Art. 33.2)

- Notification to supervisory authority (controller’s duty):
  - The controller shall notify the personal data breach to the competent supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it. (G Art. 33.1; G Rec. 85)
  - If notification cannot be made within 72 hours, the reasons for the delay should accompany the notification and information may be provided in phases without undue further delay. (G Rec. 85)
  - The notification should describe the nature of the breach and, where possible, include: the categories and approximate number of data subjects concerned and of personal data records concerned; the name and contact details of the data protection officer or other contact point; the likely consequences of the breach; and the measures taken or proposed to address and mitigate its adverse effects. (G Art. 33.3)

- Assessment, technical/organisational measures and timing:
  - The controller should ensure appropriate technological and organisational measures are in place to establish whether a breach has occurred and to inform the supervisory authority promptly; the assessment of “without undue delay” must take into account the nature and gravity of the breach and its consequences. (G Rec. 87)
  - In setting formats/procedures for notifications, consideration should be given to whether technical protections limited misuse (e.g. encryption) and to legitimate law‑enforcement interests where early disclosure could hamper investigations. (G Rec. 88)

- Communication to data subjects:
  - When the breach is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller shall communicate the breach to the data subject without undue delay. (G Art. 34.1)
  - That communication should describe the nature of the breach and give recommendations to data subjects to mitigate potential adverse effects; it should be made as soon as reasonably feasible and in close cooperation with the supervisory authority (and, where relevant, law‑enforcement authorities). (G Rec. 86)
  - Exceptions to communicating to data subjects: no communication is required if (a) appropriate technical and organisational protection measures were implemented and applied to the affected data (e.g. encryption), (b) subsequent measures ensure the high risk no longer exists, or (c) communication would involve disproportionate effort — in the last case a public communication or similar equally effective measure must be used. (G Art. 34.3)

question: What is the procedure to follow in the event of a data breach?
answer_text:
- Immediate notification to the supervisory authority: the controller shall notify the personal data breach to the supervisory authority competent in accordance with Article 55 without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it (G Art. 33.1; G Rec. 85).

- Exception where no risk: notification is not required if the controller can demonstrate, in accordance with the accountability principle, that the personal data breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons (G Rec. 85).

- If notification cannot be made within 72 hours: the reasons for the delay must accompany the notification, and information may be provided in phases without undue further delay (G Rec. 85).

- Detection and timing considerations: the controller should ensure appropriate technical and organisational measures to detect breaches and to inform the supervisory authority promptly; whether notification was made without undue delay must take into account the nature and gravity of the breach and its consequences for data subjects (G Rec. 87).

- Communication to data subjects: where the breach is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller should communicate the breach to the data subject without undue delay, describing the nature of the breach and recommendations to mitigate adverse effects; such communications should be made as soon as reasonably feasible and in close cooperation with the supervisory authority and, where relevant, law‑enforcement authorities (G Rec. 86).

- Practical/procedural safeguards and law‑enforcement interests: detailed rules on format and procedures should take into account the circumstances of the breach (including whether data were protected by technical measures) and the legitimate interests of law‑enforcement authorities where early disclosure could hamper investigations (G Rec. 88).

- Competence of the supervisory authority: each supervisory authority is competent for performing its tasks and exercising its powers on the territory of its own Member State (G Art. 55); the controller must notify the supervisory authority competent in accordance with Article 55 (G Art. 33.1).

question: Who determines disputes under a contract?
answer_text:
- The court or courts of a Member State designated by the parties to have jurisdiction shall determine disputes under the contract (B Art. 25.1; RI Rec. 12).  
- Where the parties have so agreed, that jurisdiction shall be exclusive unless the parties have agreed otherwise (B Art. 25.1).

question: Who determines disputes under a contract?
answer_text:
- One or more courts or tribunals of a Member State determine disputes under the contract when the parties agree to confer jurisdiction on them (RI Rec. 12; B Art. 25.1).  
- Where the parties have so agreed, that court or those courts “shall have jurisdiction” to settle the disputes (B Art. 25.1).

question: Who determines disputes under a contract?
answer_text: Courts or tribunals of a Member State (i.e. a court or the courts of a Member State) determine disputes under the contract where the parties have agreed to confer jurisdiction on them (RI Rec. 12; B Art. 25).

question: Who determines disputes under a contract?
answer_text: - Where the parties so agree, disputes under the contract are to be determined by one or more courts or tribunals of a Member State (agreement conferring jurisdiction) (RI Rec. 12; B Art. 25.1).

question: Who determines disputes under a contract?
answer_text:
- Disputes under the contract are to be determined by one or more courts or tribunals of a Member State when the parties so agree (RI Rec. 12; B Art. 25.1).  
- Where the parties have agreed that a court or the courts of a Member State are to settle the disputes, that court/those courts shall have jurisdiction (and that jurisdiction is exclusive unless the parties have agreed otherwise) (B Art. 25.1).

question: What factors should be taken into account for conferring the jurisdiction to determine disputes under a contract?
answer_text:
- An agreement between the parties to confer on one or more courts or tribunals of a Member State exclusive jurisdiction is a relevant factor in deciding whether a choice of law has been clearly demonstrated (RI Rec. 12).

- Formal and substantive consequences of such an agreement:
  - It confers jurisdiction on the chosen court(s) unless the agreement is null and void as to its substantive validity under the law of that Member State; the jurisdiction is exclusive unless the parties agreed otherwise (B Art. 25.1).
  - The agreement must be in writing or evidenced in writing, or in a form that accords with practices the parties have established between themselves, or—in international trade—according to a widely known and regularly observed usage (B Art. 25.1).
  - Any electronic communication providing a durable record is equivalent to “writing” (B Art. 25.2).
  - An agreement conferring jurisdiction contained in a contract is independent of the other contract terms and its validity cannot be contested solely on the ground that the contract is not valid (B Art. 25.5).

question: What factors should be taken into account for conferring the jurisdiction to determine disputes under a contract?
answer_text:
- The parties’ agreement to confer jurisdiction (in particular an agreement to confer exclusive jurisdiction on one or more courts or tribunals of a Member State) should be taken into account when determining whether a choice of law has been clearly demonstrated (RI Rec. 12).

question: Which law is applicable to a non-contractual obligation?
answer_text:
- Autonomous concept: for the purposes of the Regulation, a "non‑contractual obligation" is an autonomous concept (Rec. 11).

- Pre‑contractual dealings (culpa in contrahendo): governed by the law that applies to the contract or would have applied if the contract had been entered into (Art. 12.1). Where that law cannot be determined, the applicable law is (Art. 12.2):  
  - (a) the law of the country in which the damage occurs; or  
  - (b) if the parties have their habitual residence in the same country when the event giving rise to the damage occurs, the law of that country; or  
  - (c) if the obligation is manifestly more closely connected with another country, the law of that other country (Art. 12.2).

- Acts performed without due authority in connection with another's affairs (negotiorum gestio): if the non‑contractual obligation concerns a relationship between the parties (e.g. contractual or tortious) that is closely connected, it is governed by the law governing that relationship (Art. 11.1). Where that law cannot be determined, the applicable law is, in order (Art. 11.2–4):  
  - the law of the country of the parties' common habitual residence at the relevant time (Art. 11.2); or  
  - the law of the country in which the act was performed (Art. 11.3); or  
  - if manifestly more closely connected with another country, the law of that other country (Art. 11.4).

- Unfair competition and restrictions of competition: the law of the country where competitive relations or the collective interests of consumers are, or are likely to be, affected (Art. 6.1). Special rules apply where only a specific competitor is affected (Art. 6.2) and for restrictions of competition and multi‑State markets (Art. 6.3). Article 6.4 provides that the law chosen under Article 6 may not be derogated from by agreement pursuant to Article 14 (Art. 6.4).

- Burden of proof and presumptions: the law governing the non‑contractual obligation applies to the extent it contains rules that raise presumptions of law or determine the burden of proof; modes of proof follow Art. 22 (Art. 22.1–2).

question: Which law is applicable to a non-contractual obligation?

Short answer: the applicable law depends on the type of non‑contractual obligation; different special rules determine the governing law. (Recital 11 explains that “non‑contractual obligation” is an autonomous concept.) — Rec. 11.

Details (by subject-matter), with the provisions relied on:

  - Governed by the law that applies to the contract or that would have applied had it been concluded (Art. 12.1). — RII Art. 12
  - If that law cannot be determined, the fallback rules are: (a) law of the country where the damage occurs; or (b) if the parties share habitual residence in the same country when the event occurs, that country’s law; or (c) if manifestly more closely connected to another country, the law of that other country (Art. 12.2). — RII Art. 12

  - If not determinable on that basis and the parties share habitual residence when the event occurs, that country’s law applies (Art. 11.2). — RII Art. 11
  - If still not determinable, the law of the country in which the act was performed applies (Art. 11.3). — RII Art. 11

question: Which law is applicable to a non-contractual obligation?
answer_text:
Which law applies depends on the nature of the non‑contractual obligation. Key rules in the Regulation are:

- General rule for tort/delict: the law of the country in which the damage occurs (irrespective of where the event giving rise to the damage occurred or where indirect consequences occur). RII Art. 4.1.  
- Unfair competition: the law of the country where competitive relations or the collective interests of consumers are, or are likely to be, affected. RII Art. 6.1.  
- Pre‑contractual dealings: the law that applies to the contract or that would have applied had the contract been concluded. RII Art. 12.1.  
- Acts performed without due authority in connection with another’s affairs: if the non‑contractual obligation concerns a relationship (e.g. contract or tort/delict) closely connected with it, it is governed by the law that governs that relationship; if manifestly more closely connected with another country, the law of that other country applies. RII Art. 11.1; RII Art. 11.4.  
- Party autonomy: the parties may agree on the law governing the non‑contractual obligation (subject to the temporal and commercial limits in the Regulation and without prejudice to third‑party rights). RII Art. 14.1.  
- Scope and application notes: the Regulation treats “non‑contractual obligation” as an autonomous concept and covers strict liability (RII Rec. 11), applies also to obligations likely to arise (RII Art. 2.2), and excludes certain categories (e.g. family law, succession, negotiable instruments, company law, trusts, nuclear damage, privacy/defamation) from its scope (RII Art. 1.2). RII Rec. 11; RII Art. 2.2; RII Art. 1.2.  
- Effects of the applicable law: the law so chosen governs matters such as basis and extent of liability, grounds for exemption, assessment of damage, transferability of claims, persons entitled to compensation, prescription/limitation rules, and related procedural measures within the court’s powers. RII Art. 15.15.

question: What factors should be taken into account for conferring the jurisdiction to determine disputes under a consumer contract?
answer_text:
- The nature of the contract: whether it is (a) a sale of goods on instalment credit terms, (b) a loan repayable by instalments or other credit made to finance the sale of goods, or (c) another contract concluded with a trader who pursues commercial/professional activities in the consumer’s Member State or directs such activities to that State (and the contract falls within those activities) (B Art. 17.1(a)–(c)).

- The domicile/place of parties: a consumer may sue either in the courts of the Member State where the other party is domiciled or in the courts for the place where the consumer is domiciled; conversely, proceedings may be brought against a consumer only in the courts of the Member State where the consumer is domiciled (B Art. 18.1–2).

- Whether the trader has a branch, agency or other establishment in a Member State: a trader not domiciled in a Member State but having such an establishment there is deemed domiciled in that Member State for disputes arising out of the operations of that establishment (B Art. 17.2).

- Whether the trader’s activity is “directed” to the consumer’s Member State and the contract was concluded within the framework of those activities; for distance/Internet sales, mere accessibility of a website is not sufficient — relevant factors include whether the site solicits distance contracts and whether a contract has actually been concluded at a distance (RI Rec. 24).

- Exceptions and limits: the consumer-jurisdiction rules do not apply to certain transport contracts (except combined travel/accommodation) (B Art. 17.3), and the Section’s rules may be departed from only in the limited cases listed by agreement (B Art. 19.1).

- Where the defendant is not domiciled in a Member State, jurisdiction of each Member State’s courts is determined by the law of that Member State, subject to the consumer-protection rule (B Art. 6.1).

- Where proceedings may be brought by the consumer: either in the courts of the Member State in which the other party is domiciled or in the courts for the place where the consumer is domiciled (B Art. 18.1). Proceedings against a consumer may be brought only in the courts of the Member State in which the consumer is domiciled (B Art. 18.2).

- Factors specific to distance-selling / “directed activity” (interpretation to be harmonised with Regulation (EC) No 44/2001): whether the trader’s activities are directed to the consumer’s Member State and the contract was concluded within the framework of those activities; mere accessibility of an Internet site is not sufficient; relevant is whether the site solicits conclusion of distance contracts and a contract has actually been concluded at a distance; the language or currency used by a website is not a relevant factor (RI Rec. 24).

- Parties’ agreement can displace these provisions only in the limited cases set out (agreement entered into after the dispute has arisen; an agreement allowing the consumer to sue in other courts; or an agreement at contract conclusion conferring jurisdiction of the courts of the Member State where both parties are domiciled/habitually resident), subject to conditions (B Art. 19.1).

question: What factors should be taken into account for conferring the jurisdiction to determine disputes under a consumer contract?

question: What factors should be taken into account for conferring the jurisdiction to determine disputes under a consumer contract?
